I work as a nanny, and last summer I interviewed for a new position. My potential charges were 1 and 3 years old (both boys), and I met them and their mother in a nearby park/playground so we could all get to know each other.

I arrived early and sat on a bench enjoying the fresh air and warm weather. Soon I saw them arriving and went to greet them and introduce myself. My first thought was, "Thank god they're all normal sized"! (I've worked for fatties in the past and it's a nightmare being expected to indulge the kids with all kinds of chips, sodas, and sugary treats for their after school snacks while they gape at the TV (not to mention having my place of employment be a literal pig sty).

The 3-year-old and I hit it off and we ran around the playground for a while. (Thin privilege is being able to easily keep up with young children even when you're in your mid-50s.) The mother and I talked, and it was overall a delightful hour or so. When things winded down and we walked together back to our cars, the 3-year-old began skipping ahead of us and chanting loudly, "Not fat! Not fat!" over and over.

I stifled a laugh but wasn't sure why he was saying this and I guess the mother caught my look of confusion. When I caught her eye to see what she made of her son's behavior, she looked really embarrassed and said, "I am so sorry! This is embarrassing and I'm not sure how to explain it, but... well... I think he's relieved you're not fat!". I burst out laughing and said something about how kids have no censor and will just say what's on their mind, they don't know they're being rude (although I didn't see his behavior as rude at all, I loved it haha), I wasn't offended, etc.

She looked relieved and said, "He loves most of the teachers at his preschool... well not most, but some of them. Actually a lot of them are pretty heavy and he says the fat ones are always mean to the kids and now he has decided that he doesn't like fat people and I guess he was worried -- before we met -- that you would be fat and therefore "mean".

She looked mortified to be explaining it, but I just kept a small smile and nodded my head to let her know that I wasn't the least bit offended. (I am tiny myself.)

I ended up being offered, and accepting, the position and I could not be happier. I am absolutely crazy about this family and the best part is they're all human-sized, with the splendid lifestyle to boot.

#Strength, Hypertrophy, and Exercise Descriptions

I've set this up as a split routine, so you do A for the first day, then alternate. The first two sets of each exercise are meant to be for warming/ramping up. You can skip those if you want. The + indicates the exercises are paired and you don't need to rest between them. Rest times between pairs of exercises are:30s-2 minutes for hypertrophy, 5-7 minutes for strength. 9+ minutes if you have all day or are simply exhausted. The number of reps is based on the relative difficulty of each exercise, you should play around with it to see what works for you.

When starting out, you'll want to move slowly through the progressions, and reduce the number of sets for the first week of training so you're not too sore to do the next session. The first two sets of each exercise are meant to be for warming/ramping up. You can skip those if you want. The + indicates the exercises are paired and you don't need to rest between them. Rest times between pairs of exercises are:30s-2 minutes for hypertrophy, 5-7 minutes for strength. 9+ minutes if you have all day or are simply exhausted.

If you can't do an exercise for the suggested number of reps, you might consider either changing the number of repetitions, or if your goals are more hypertrophy oriented, you may do however many reps you can do, then switch to an easier exercise to finish the set. Like do 3 close push-ups and finish the set with 5 regular push-ups. With the unilateral (single limb) exercises, I suggest doing the full set on 1 limb, then repeating with the opposite limb. You may also switch limbs in between each rep, which will allow you to squeeze out a few more repetitions at the expense of hypertrophy.

The *Hanging Leg Raises* in A are entirely skippable if you have lower back issues (if that's the case, do the *bridge* progression instead) have trouble keeping your scapula tight, or if you simply don't like them. The isometric portion of the routine should be enough core training at this point anyway. You may substitute [*Sliding Bridge Curls*](https://voat.co/v/bodyweightfitness/comments/453756) for the Glute-Ham Raises if you don't have a place to do them. For B I suggest you alternate rowing and dipping exercises per session. Or you just pick whatever is convenient. Alternate Chin-ups and Pull-ups per set. ~~~ A.

Push-up progression 5x8 +Squat progression 5x10

Chin-up progression 5*5 + Hanging Leg Raise Progression 5*5

B.

Lunge Progression 5*10 + Handstand Push-up progression 5*5

Glute-Ham Curl Progression 5*5 +Row/Dip Progression 5*8 ~~~

If you have isolation exercises you want to do, add them here. Anything from sissy squats, bicep curls, tricep kickbacks, whatever. I don't recommend these, but I can't stop you either. Adding Fingertip push-ups and towel hang chin-ups when you're ready will be all the grip specific work you need.

[Training your neck comes later, but here's a guide to it anyway. It would go before the strength portion.](https://voat.co/v/bodyweightfitness/comments/506162)

Adding weight: as tricky as single-leg squats are, they don't produce quite the same effect as weighted squats. If you have access to barbells, the solution is simple: Do low-bar back squats, or bulgarian split squats instead of your usual squat/lunge exercise. Deadlift instead of doing the glute-ham raise or bridge curl. Or simply replace the whole routine with weight training, get the best of both worlds. You don't need to use the Sumo stance or alternate grip. If you can't do a regular double-overhand grip on the bar, your not training your grip enough. You could use a fat bar. it makes for a hell of a grip workout.

Alternatively, you can find an object that's heavy enough to be hard to lift and pick that up a bunch of times. While I don't advocate weighting the pistol squat, except with very light weights due to the rounding in the lower back, Bulgarian split squats respond very well to loading. Sand bags, furniture, large rocks, whatever. I hope you can find a heavy object. If you can't, you can still make good progress with "pure" lower body calisthenics.

#Descriptions, Cues, and Progressions: You'll still want to look up videos of these. The "cue" is simply a short directive that helps you perform the exercise correctly. I find them useful for some reason.

Push-ups: *Bend the floor in half!*

You can manipulate a ton of things. If you find the routine puts too much stress on your wrists, doing the early progressions on your knuckles will reduce the strain. At the cost of hurting your knuckles. Do them on your fingertips for extra grip training.

On knees ->push-up ->Close/Wide ->Diamond ->Overlap -> Roman->1 Arm (*Rocky* Style, but without the jump) -> 1-arm *Bruce Lee* Style

Squats ->"Spread the floor apart with your legs/Clench your cheeks together! Wall Squats (Face the wall squats.) These are a surprisingly useful exercise to teach the hip hinge, and force you to maintain a good back angle. Stand with your knees, toes and nose right up against a wall, squat. Feels weird, right?

Close Squats: Squat with your legs close together. Assisted pistol squat: Use a door frame or something. Full pistol squat: I don't suggest adding weight to this one unless you can do it without rounding your lower back.

Lunge->Bulgarian Split Squat -> Skater Squat ->Shrimp Squat

The Bulgarian split squat is normally done with the rear foot elevated on a weight bench, but a platform 4-6 inches off the ground is the method traditionally used by Eastern European weightlifters. I like the one with the bench.

Chin-ups->*Pull your scapulae up/Pull the bar towards you*

One handed variation-not really substantially harder than a regular chin-up. Just grab your wrist with one hand and hands between sets. This improves grip strength. Wrapping a towel around the bar also creates a killer grip workout.
